raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in the myocardium, producing increased wall thickness, diastolic dysfunction, conduction disease, arrhythmias, and ultimately restrictive heart failure. Contemporary nomenclature defines amyloid by fibril precursor protein; in practice, nearly all clinically important cardiac disease is due to immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL) or transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) [1]. AL arises from a usually small plasma-cell clone and is a medical emergency because direct light-chain cardiotoxicity and rapid progression can lead to early death [2]. ATTR results from misfolding of transthyretin, either wild-type ATTR or hereditary variants, and was historically under-recognized as “senile” amyloidosis [3]. Population data established AL as rare, but modern imaging has revealed that ATTR cardiomyopathy is substantially more common than previously appreciated [4].

The clinical phenotype overlaps with common cardiovascular syndromes, which explains diagnostic delay. Patients may present with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, low-flow aortic stenosis, atrial arrhythmias, syncope, pseudo-infarct electrocardiographic patterns, low voltage relative to wall thickness, neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, biceps tendon rupture, or spinal stenosis [5], [6]. Comparative cohorts show that AL often has lower voltages, higher natriuretic peptides, and worse short-term prognosis than ATTR despite less hypertrophy, whereas ATTR tends to affect older men and progresses more indolently [7], [8]. Wild-type ATTR has been reported in a meaningful proportion of older patients labeled as HFpEF [9], and autopsy studies demonstrate frequent occult transthyretin deposits in the very elderly [10]. ATTR is also enriched among patients undergoing transcatheter aortic-valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis [11] and can be detected years before overt cardiomyopathy in tenosynovial tissue from carpal tunnel surgery [12].

Diagnosis requires both recognition of the cardiac phenotype and precise amyloid typing. Echocardiography commonly shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, and reduced longitudinal function despite preserved ejection fraction. Tissue Doppler and strain imaging demonstrated early longitudinal dysfunction in AL [13], and relative apical sparing of longitudinal strain is a useful diagnostic clue, although not pathognomonic [14]. Cardiac magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: global subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and abnormal gadolinium kinetics are characteristic [15]. Native T1 mapping and extracellular volume quantification detect diffuse infiltration and help quantify burden [16], while late gadolinium enhancement and T1-derived measures provide prognostic information [17], [18].

Bone-avid tracer scintigraphy transformed ATTR diagnosis. Early work with technetium-labeled DPD showed strong myocardial uptake in ATTR compared with AL [19], and pyrophosphate imaging similarly distinguished transthyretin from light-chain disease [20]. In patients with typical cardiac imaging, grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake on bone scintigraphy can establish ATTR cardiomyopathy noninvasively only when monoclonal protein testing is negative [21]. Therefore, every suspected case requires serum and urine immunofixation plus serum free light chains; if a monoclonal protein is present, tissue confirmation and amyloid typing, ideally by mass spectrometry, are needed to avoid misclassifying AL as ATTR.

Risk stratification is biomarker centered. In AL, cardiac troponins and NT-proBNP define stage and identify patients at highest early mortality [22]. Incorporation of the involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference refines prognosis and reflects clonal burden [23]. In wild-type ATTR, staging systems using natriuretic peptides, troponin, and renal function stratify survival and support treatment discussions [24], [25]. Prognosis also depends on functional class, renal impairment, arrhythmias, hypotension, and extracardiac involvement.

Management combines amyloid-specific therapy, careful heart-failure care, and rhythm management. Diuretics are the cornerstone for congestion, but patients are preload dependent and often poorly tolerate beta-blockers, renin–angiotensin inhibitors, and nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers. In AL, urgent plasma-cell therapy is essential. Daratumumab added to cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone improves hematologic and organ responses in newly diagnosed AL [26], while bortezomib-based regimens established rapid clonal control as a central strategy [27]. Selected patients may undergo autologous stem-cell transplantation, but advanced cardiac involvement increases treatment risk.

For ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis, a transthyretin stabilizer, reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization and slowed functional decline in a pivotal randomized trial [28]. Gene-silencing therapies have expanded options in hereditary ATTR; patisiran improved cardiac structure and function measures in patients with hereditary ATTR and cardiac involvement [29], and inotersen improved neurologic outcomes in hereditary ATTR, with cardiac applications continuing to evolve [30]. Earlier diagnosis is now the major unmet need: applying simple red-flag algorithms, ruling out AL promptly, and using scintigraphy appropriately can convert cardiac amyloidosis from a late fatal diagnosis into a treatable cardiomyopathy.
